# ============================================================================= # Policy Priorities: a benefit-cost ranking of 60 policies # Tyler Young · Lighthearted Humans thesis project # # Runs as a normal Shiny app in RStudio (Run App) and is exported to the # website with shinylive (see R/03_export_dashboard.R), where it runs entirely # in the visitor's browser. Base R graphics and plain HTML tables only (no # ggplot2 or DT), so the browser has far less to download. # ============================================================================= library(shiny) library(bslib) source("bca_engine.R") pol <- read.csv("policies.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) src <- read.csv("sources.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) cats <- sort(unique(pol$category)) esc <- function(x) htmltools::htmlEscape(ifelse(is.na(x), "", as.character(x))) fmt_bcr <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "—", ifelse(abs(x) >= 100, formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ","), ifelse(abs(x) >= 10, formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1), formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)))) fmt_bn <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "—", ifelse(x < 0, paste0("saves $", trimws(formatC(-x, format = "fg", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")), "B"), ifelse(x == 0, "$0", ifelse(x >= 1000, paste0("$", formatC(x / 1000, format = "f", digits = 1), "T"), paste0("$", trimws(formatC(x, format = "fg", digits = 3, big.mark = ",")), "B"))))) fmt_pct <- function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%") badge <- function(g) sprintf('%s', GRADE_COLS[g], ifelse(g %in% c("A-", "B+", "B", "B-", "C-"), "#2d3a4a", "#ffffff"), esc(g)) src_link <- function(url, doi) { u <- ifelse(!is.na(doi) & nzchar(doi), paste0("https://doi.org/", sub("^https?://(dx\\.)?doi\\.org/", "", doi)), url) ifelse(is.na(u) | !nzchar(u), "", sprintf(' link', esc(u))) } DIFF_COLS <- c(easy = unname(PAL["blue"]), moderate = unname(PAL["yellow"]), hard = unname(PAL["red"])) WHO_LABEL <- c(`pro-poor` = "Mostly the poor", broad = "Everyone", regressive = "Mostly the better-off") TYPE_LABEL <- c(peer_reviewed = "Peer-reviewed", book = "Book", working_paper = "Working paper", think_tank = "Think tank", government = "Government", intl_org = "International body") # ---- Grading rubric (shown on the Uncertainty tab; ODA <- c(`2023` = 223.7, `2024` = 214.6, `2025` = 174.3, `2026` = 174.3 * (1 - 0.058)) AVAIL_YR <- ODA[["2025"]] # latest actual year CONTEXT <- data.frame( what = c("Global fossil-fuel subsidies, 2024 (explicit $725B plus unpriced pollution and climate costs)", "UN estimate of the yearly gap to fund the Sustainable Development Goals (2026 report)", "Global climate finance, 2025 (estimate)", "Official development aid from rich-country donors, 2025", "World Bank Group lending commitments to partner countries, fiscal 2025", "US official development aid, 2025 (down 57% from 2024)"), bn = c(7400, 4000, 2100, ODA[["2025"]], 118.5, 29.0), source = c("IMF Working Paper 25/270 (2025 update)", "UN Financing for Sustainable Development Report 2026", "Climate Policy Initiative, Global Landscape of Climate Finance 2026", "OECD, preliminary 2025 ODA data (April 2026)", "World Bank Group Annual Report 2025", "OECD, preliminary 2025 ODA data (April 2026)"), url = c("https://www.elibrary.imf.org/view/journals/001/2025/270/article-A001-en.xml", "https://desapublications.un.org/publications/financing-sustainable-development-report-2026", "https://glcf.climatepolicyinitiative.org/", "https://www.oecd.org/en/data/insights/data-explainers/2026/04/a-historic-decline-in-foreign-aid-preliminary-2025-oda-data.html", "https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/annual-report/financial-summary", "https://www.oecd.org/en/data/insights/data-explainers/2026/04/a-historic-decline-in-foreign-aid-preliminary-2025-oda-data.html"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE) context_ui <- local({ mx <- log10(max(CONTEXT$bn)) rows <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(CONTEXT)), function(i) sprintf( '%s

name: bca_engine.R
content:
# =============================================================================
# bca_engine.R: the analysis engine for the Lighthearted Humans policy ranking
#
# A comparative benefit-cost analysis built on published estimates. Adding
# income, feasibility, evidence and cost criteria makes it a multi-criteria
# decision analysis (MCDA). Every number comes from the published sources in
# data/raw/evidence_v3.json. The same code drives the paper (02_run_analysis.R)
# and the dashboard (app/app.R). Base R only, so it runs fast in the browser.
#
# Pipeline for one set of settings:
#   1. shrink_by_grade()   evidence-quality adjustment (skepticism dial)
#   2. time_adjust()       re-express at a different discount rate
#   3. simulate()          Monte Carlo over each policy's range (1,000 draws)
#   4. criteria_matrix()   value, who benefits, feasibility, cost
#   5. mcda_score()        benefit-cost value plus optional preference tilts
#   6. rank_stats()        how often each policy finishes in the top 10
#   7. portfolio()         which policies clear a benefit-cost threshold
#      worst_n()           the counterfactual: fund the 10 worst instead
# =============================================================================

N_SIMS <- 1000     # Monte Carlo draws: fixed, stated on the dashboard
TOP_N  <- 20       # "chance of finishing in the top 20"

GRADES <- c("A+", "A", "A-", "B+", "B", "B-", "C+", "C", "C-")
GRADE_WEIGHT <- setNames(c(1.00, 0.95, 0.90, 0.85, 0.80, 0.75, 0.70, 0.65, 0.60), GRADES)
# Faded red / yellow / blue triad: A grades blue, B grades yellow, C grades red
GRADE_COLS <- setNames(c("#3d6fd6", "#5b8def", "#8db0f3", "#c9982e", "#e3b453", "#efd08a",
                         "#c75b5b", "#e07a7a", "#eca7a7"), GRADES)
PAL <- c(blue = "#5b8def", blue_lt = "#a8c5f7", yellow = "#f2c46d", red = "#e07a7a",
         green = "#76bf94", ink = "#2d3a4a")
FEAS_SCORE <- c(easy = 1, moderate = 0.5, hard = 0)
WHO_SCORE  <- c(`pro-poor` = 1, broad = 0.5, regressive = 0)

# --- 1. Evidence-quality shrinkage -------------------------------------------
# Weaker evidence pulls a ratio toward break-even (1:1).
#   Positive ratios shrink in log space:  BCR^k      (k = 1 - s(1 - w_grade))
#   Zero or negative ratios shrink toward zero, i.e. toward break-even and away
#   from net harm:  k * BCR. Both branches are continuous and never cross 1.
# skepticism s = 0 ignores evidence quality; 1 applies the full grade weights.
shrink_by_grade <- function(bcr, grade, skepticism = 0.5) {
  w <- GRADE_WEIGHT[grade]; w[is.na(w)] <- min(GRADE_WEIGHT)
  k <- 1 - skepticism * (1 - w)
  out <- ifelse(bcr > 0, exp(k * log(pmax(bcr, 1e-12))), k * bcr)
  out[is.na(bcr)] <- NA
  unname(out)
}

# --- 2. Discount-rate re-expression -------------------------------------------
# Published ratios are already discounted, mostly at 3-8% (5% is typical).
# If benefits arrive on average `lag` years after costs, re-expressing at
# `rate` multiplies the ratio by ((1 + base_rate) / (1 + rate))^lag.
time_adjust <- function(bcr, rate = 0.05, base_rate = 0.05, lag = 10) {
  bcr * ((1 + base_rate) / (1 + rate))^lag
}

# --- 3. Monte Carlo ------------------------------------------------------------
# Each published range is treated as a 90% interval of a lognormal. Ranges that
# touch or cross zero use a normal instead.
simulate <- function(lo, hi, n = N_SIMS, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)
  out <- matrix(NA_real_, n, length(lo))
  for (j in seq_along(lo)) {
    a <- lo[j]; b <- hi[j]
    if (is.na(a) || is.na(b)) next
    if (a > 0 || b < 0) {
      s  <- if (a > 0) 1 else -1
      la <- log(abs(a)); lb <- log(abs(b))
      out[, j] <- s * exp(rnorm(n, (la + lb) / 2, max(abs(lb - la) / (2 * 1.645), 0.10)))
    } else {
      out[, j] <- rnorm(n, (a + b) / 2, max((b - a) / (2 * 1.645), 0.05))
    }
  }
  out
}

# Signed log so harms and benefits sit on one comparable scale
slog <- function(x) sign(x) * log10(1 + abs(x))

# --- 4. Criteria (all 0-1, higher is better) ------------------------------------
rescale01 <- function(x) {
  r <- range(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  if (!all(is.finite(r)) || diff(r) == 0) return(rep(0.5, length(x)))
  (x - r[1]) / diff(r)
}

criteria_matrix <- function(p, bcr_point) {
  cost <- pmax(ifelse(is.na(p$cost_bn), 0, p$cost_bn), 0)   # savings count as zero cost
  data.frame(
    value       = rescale01(slog(bcr_point)),
    equity      = unname(ifelse(is.na(WHO_SCORE[p$who_benefits]), 0.5, WHO_SCORE[p$who_benefits])),
    feasibility = unname(ifelse(is.na(FEAS_SCORE[p$difficulty]), 0, FEAS_SCORE[p$difficulty])),
    cost        = 1 - rescale01(log10(1 + cost))
  )
}

# --- 5. Score: benefit-cost value plus optional tilts ------------------------------
# The benefit-cost value always counts in full. Each other criterion can tilt the
# score toward one end or the other: tilt runs from -1 to +1 (0 = no effect), and
# a full tilt counts TILT_MAX times as much as the benefit-cost value.
TILT_MAX <- 0.3
TILT_NAMES <- c("equity", "feasibility", "cost")   # evidence enters through skepticism, not a tilt

tilt_part <- function(C, tilts) {
  t <- tilts[TILT_NAMES]; t[is.na(t)] <- 0
  as.vector((as.matrix(C[, TILT_NAMES]) - 0.5) %*% (TILT_MAX * unname(t)))
}
mcda_score <- function(C, tilts = c()) {
  C$value + as.vector(tilt_part(C, tilts))
}

# --- 6. Rank statistics across draws -------------------------------------------------
rank_stats <- function(score_draws, top_n = TOP_N) {
  R <- t(apply(score_draws, 1, function(s) rank(-s, ties.method = "random")))
  data.frame(p_top    = colMeans(R <= top_n),
             rank_med = apply(R, 2, stats::median),
             rank_lo  = apply(R, 2, stats::quantile, 0.05),
             rank_hi  = apply(R, 2, stats::quantile, 0.95))
}

# --- Main entry point ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Returns one row per policy, best first.
# tilts: named vector with any of equity, feasibility, evidence, cost in [-1, 1];
#        positive favours the poor / easy / strong evidence / cheap.
run_bca <- function(p, skepticism = 0.5, rate = 0.05, base_rate = 0.05, lag = 10,
                    tilts = c(equity = 0, feasibility = 0, cost = 0),
                    n_sims = N_SIMS, seed = 42, top_n = TOP_N) {
  p <- p[p$rated, , drop = FALSE]
  draws <- simulate(p$bcr_low, p$bcr_high, n_sims, seed)
  D <- t(apply(draws, 1, function(x)
    time_adjust(shrink_by_grade(x, p$grade, skepticism), rate, base_rate, lag)))
  med <- apply(D, 2, stats::median)
  C <- criteria_matrix(p, med)
  score <- mcda_score(C, tilts)

  # Rank uncertainty: re-score every draw (value varies, tilts fixed)
  other <- as.vector(tilt_part(C, tilts))
  rng <- range(slog(med))
  S <- t(apply(D, 1, function(x) (slog(x) - rng[1]) / max(diff(rng), 1e-9) + other))
  rs <- rank_stats(S, top_n)

  out <- data.frame(p[, c("id", "title", "short", "category", "grade", "difficulty",
                          "who_benefits", "cost_bn", "bcr_low", "bcr_high")],
                    bcr_median = med,
                    bcr_q05 = apply(D, 2, stats::quantile, 0.05),
                    bcr_q95 = apply(D, 2, stats::quantile, 0.95),
                    C, score = score, rs, row.names = NULL)
  out <- out[order(-out$score), ]
  out$rank <- seq_len(nrow(out))
  rownames(out) <- NULL
  out
}

# --- 7. Budget: every policy that clears a benefit-cost threshold ------------------
portfolio <- function(res, min_bcr = 1) {
  f <- res[res$bcr_median >= min_bcr, ]
  f <- f[order(-f$bcr_median), ]
  f$cost_used  <- pmax(ifelse(is.na(f$cost_bn), 0, f$cost_bn), 0)
  f$benefit_bn <- f$cost_used * f$bcr_median
  f$net_bn     <- f$benefit_bn - f$cost_used
  f
}

# Counterfactual: the n policies with the lowest adjusted ratio
# Policies whose benefits overlap (nested or shared mechanism). In the budget
# exercise only the highest-ranked member of each group is funded.
OVERLAP <- list(c(9, 10), c(39, 43, 47), c(52, 54), c(1, 20, 22, 25, 42))

# Greedy allocation: fund policies with ratio >= min_bcr in descending order of
# ratio, skipping any that no longer fit or that overlap one already funded.
fund_budget <- function(res, budget, min_bcr = 1) {
  r <- res[res$bcr_median >= min_bcr & !is.na(res$cost_bn) & res$cost_bn > 0, ]
  r <- r[order(-r$bcr_median), ]
  left <- budget; k <- logical(nrow(r)); taken <- integer(0)
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(r))) {
    grp <- unlist(Filter(function(g) r$id[i] %in% g, OVERLAP))
    if (length(grp) && any(taken %in% setdiff(grp, r$id[i]))) next
    if (r$cost_bn[i] <= left) { k[i] <- TRUE; left <- left - r$cost_bn[i]; taken <- c(taken, r$id[i]) }
  }
  f <- r[k, ]
  f$spend <- f$cost_bn; f$net <- f$spend * (f$bcr_median - 1)
  f
}

# Counterfactual: the same amount spread equally across the costed policies
# among the n lowest-ratio policies.
fund_worst <- function(res, amount, n = 10) {
  w <- res[order(res$bcr_median), ][seq_len(min(n, nrow(res))), ]
  w <- w[!is.na(w$cost_bn) & w$cost_bn > 0, ]
  w$spend <- amount / nrow(w); w$net <- w$spend * (w$bcr_median - 1)
  w
}

worst_n <- function(res, n = 10) {
  f <- res[order(res$bcr_median), ][seq_len(min(n, nrow(res))), ]
  f$cost_used  <- pmax(ifelse(is.na(f$cost_bn), 0, f$cost_bn), 0)
  f$benefit_bn <- f$cost_used * f$bcr_median
  f$net_bn     <- f$benefit_bn - f$cost_used
  f
}

name: methodology.html
content:
3.1 Research design

This study is a comparative benefit-cost analysis (BCA) built on published estimates. It does not produce new primary estimates of benefits and costs. Instead, it assembles benefit-cost ratios (BCRs) from existing studies and official reports, puts them on a common scale, and ranks the policies. This follows the approach of the Copenhagen Consensus projects (Lomborg, 2014, 2023; Copenhagen Consensus Center, 2023), which also rank interventions by published or commissioned BCRs.

The design departs from a single-criterion BCA in two ways. First, evidence quality, uncertainty and time preference are modelled explicitly rather than taken at face value. Second, four further criteria (who benefits, feasibility, strength of evidence and cost) are carried alongside the BCR. Adding these criteria makes the study a multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA; Keeney & Raiffa, 1976; Belton & Stewart, 2002).

The BCR remains the primary criterion throughout. The other criteria can shift a policy’s score only within a bounded margin (Section 3.9), so the ranking cannot be driven by arbitrary weights.

The analysis answers three questions:

  1. What order of priority do the published estimates imply?
  2. How robust is that order to the quality of the evidence, to the discount rate and to the reader’s preferences?
  3. What would a fixed budget buy if allocated by that order, compared with allocating it to the lowest-ranked policies?

Perspective and standing. The intended perspective is global: benefits and costs count wherever they fall. In practice each ratio inherits the standing of its source. Most trade, health and development estimates are global or cover low- and middle-income countries, while many regulatory and tax estimates are for the United States or the European Union. Where a constructed ratio combines components with different standing, this is noted in the policy’s documentation. Benefits are measured as each source measures them (welfare, consumer surplus, GDP, lives valued with a value of statistical life, or fiscal savings). No common price year, currency conversion or value of statistical life was imposed. Ratios are unit-free, so a common price year matters less than it would for net present values, but mixed standing and benefit concepts remain a limitation (Section 3.13).

3.2 Policy selection

Sixty policies were selected to span the main strategies proposed for raising living standards. The largest area groups are:

  • Health: 11 policies, including the Copenhagen Consensus “best buys” in health.
  • Climate and mandates: 11 policies, the climate and social mandates proposed by governments and international bodies.
  • Energy: 7 policies.
  • Education: 6 policies.
  • Science and innovation: 6 policies.

Money and finance, governance and tax, and land and property contribute 5 policies each, and trade 4.

Selection was purposive, not random. The list was designed to put market-liberalising reforms (free trade, sound money, deregulation, property rights) on the same scale as aid-funded interventions and regulatory mandates. These reforms are rarely included in priority-setting exercises. Each policy is defined by a short title stating its scope, for example “Unilateral global free trade: zero tariffs, zero quotas.”

Several policies overlap: their benefits are nested or share a mechanism, so they are not additive. There are four overlap groups:

  • neonatal hospital upgrades and maternal-newborn packages (#9, #10);
  • occupational licensing, teacher certification and degree accreditation (#39, #43, #47);
  • the Green New Deal and the 15-minute-city bundle, which contains it (#52, #54);
  • unilateral free trade and the narrower trade reforms it contains: trade facilitation, Jones Act repeal, agricultural subsidies and anti-dumping duties (#1, #20, #22, #25, #42).

In the budget exercise only the highest-ranked member of each group is funded (Section 3.11). In the ranking, each policy is shown on its own, as a separate option.

3.3 Evidence search and source selection

For each policy, a targeted literature search was run using academic databases, Google Scholar, NBER, SSRN, institutional repositories and the publications of research institutes. The search looked for four kinds of evidence:

  1. published BCRs or net-present-value estimates of the policy or a close analogue;
  2. quantified benefits (welfare, GDP, lives, prices) and quantified costs that can be combined into a ratio;
  3. evidence on who gains and loses;
  4. evidence on implementation, meaning legal requirements and precedents.

Sources were ranked by study type:

  1. peer-reviewed articles first;
  2. then official estimates (CBO, JCT, OMB, EPA and other regulators, the IMF, OECD, World Bank and UN agencies);
  3. then working papers, books by economists, and think-tank studies with stated methods.

Every source was checked by opening the publication or its landing page, and no citation was recorded without a verifiable URL or DOI. The final register holds 693 evidence records (621 unique works) and 32 counter-evidence records, or 648 unique works in all. Of the evidence records:

  • 293 peer-reviewed articles;
  • 74 government reports;
  • 45 reports from international organisations;
  • 44 working papers;
  • 28 books;
  • 173 think-tank studies;
  • 36 other published items, mainly news and press reports.

The search was a structured targeted review, not a systematic review in the PRISMA sense (Page et al., 2021). The book this study accompanies argues for economic freedom. Consistent with that argument, the search deliberately sought out authors who estimate the dynamic, long-run gains of market reforms: growth effects rather than static welfare triangles alone. Examples include Anderson (2015) and Wacziarg & Welch (2008) on trade, Dawson & Seater (2013) on regulation, and Duranton & Puga (2023) on land-use rules.

To keep this choice transparent, studies were set aside from a policy’s range only when a written reason was recorded. The typical reasons were that a study measured a narrower or different version of the policy, used a partial or static model, or covered only one country or episode. All such studies are kept in a counter-evidence register (Appendix B), shown with the policy in the Policy explorer. This lets a reader rebuild each range with the excluded studies included. The register currently covers 16 of the 60 policies, and the most consequential exclusions are tested directly in Section 3.10.

3.4 Extraction and construction of benefit-cost ratios

Each policy is assigned a range [L, H] for its BCR, meaning the present value of benefits divided by the present value of costs. The range is filled in one of three ways, in order of preference:

  1. Reported ratios. Where a study reports a BCR for the policy or its close equivalent, that value is used, and the range spans the credible reported estimates.
  2. Constructed ratios. Where no ratio is reported, one is constructed from published components (for example, a peer-reviewed estimate of the welfare gain divided by an official estimate of the implementation cost). The arithmetic and every input are recorded with the policy.
  3. Benefit transfer by analogy. Where the policy has never been implemented, the ratio is transferred from the closest analogue with published estimates (Johnston et al., 2015). An example is the occupational-licensing estimates of Kleiner & Soltas (2023), applied to teacher certification. Ratios built this way receive the lowest evidence grades (Section 3.5).

For policies whose induced harms exceed their benefits, a negative ratio is allowed. It is constructed as (benefits − induced damages) / cost. Damages here include, for example, excess mortality from higher energy prices or emissions added by non-additional offsets. The construction is documented for each case.

Transfers and redistribution are handled following the marginal-value-of-public-funds framework (Hendren & Sprung-Keyser, 2020). Revenue returned to taxpayers is a transfer, not a resource cost; the deadweight loss of taxation is a real cost (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley, 1985; Feldstein, 1999).

The sources do not share a common price year, currency, discount rate or time horizon. The ratios are unit-free, but these differences remain a source of heterogeneity (Section 3.13). No ratio was adjusted except as described in Sections 3.7 and 3.8.

3.5 Evidence grading

Each policy is graded on a nine-level scale according to the strongest evidence that supports its range. The scale is adapted from the logic of the GRADE framework in health research (Guyatt et al., 2008): study design sets the starting level, and indirectness lowers it.

Grade Evidence
A+ Several peer-reviewed BCAs, including randomised or controlled trials, with consistent, statistically significant results
A Peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimates backed by controlled or quasi-experimental studies
A− One peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimate, or a peer-reviewed meta-analysis whose effects convert directly into a BCR
B+ Peer-reviewed natural experiments or historical comparisons that measure the size of the gain
B Published economic theory in peer-reviewed journals or academic books, supported by historical cases and quantified in published models
B− Official estimates from governments or international bodies
C+ Think-tank studies with stated methods and numbers
C Books and published arguments using historical illustration, with numbers from secondary estimates
C− Theory only: never tried at scale, ratio built by analogy

The resulting distribution is:

Grade Policies
A+ 1
A 8
A− 13
B+ 6
B 12
B− 11
C+ 4
C 1
C− 4

3.6 Cost, distribution and feasibility ratings

Cost. Cost is the new government spending, or the mandated compliance spending, needed to carry out the policy, in US dollars per year. Two kinds of cost are excluded from this criterion:

  • Tax revenue returned to taxpayers. This is a transfer.
  • Private adjustment costs, such as displaced workers after tariffs fall. These are already inside the denominator of the ratio.

A repeal of a tariff, tax or regulation is therefore costed at zero unless a source identifies an implementation cost; 28 policies are costed at zero. For the policies re-costed under this rule, where sources disagreed the mean of the sourced figures was used. This convention is asymmetric by design: a repeal requires no spending, while a mandate requires the spending it compels. Because compliance costs of mandates enter the cost criterion and the budget totals, the convention makes mandates look more expensive than repeals, and readers should interpret the cost criterion with that in mind.

Who benefits. Each policy is rated as benefiting mostly the poor, everyone, or mostly higher incomes, from the distributional evidence in its sources. For example, trade gains concentrate in low-income countries (Anderson, 2015), and energy mandates are regressive because energy is a larger share of poor households’ budgets.

Feasibility. Feasibility is rated with a single rule applied to all 60 policies:

  • Easy: one agency, regulator or funder can act under existing law, and a precedent exists.
  • Moderate: requires ordinary legislation in one country, or a funding scale-up, and a working precedent exists somewhere.
  • Hard: requires a constitutional amendment, a binding agreement among many countries, or the dismantling of a major institution with no modern precedent.

The resulting counts are 7 easy, 34 moderate and 19 hard. The sourced reason for each rating is recorded with the policy.

3.7 Adjustments for evidence quality and time

Evidence-quality adjustment. Estimates from weaker designs tend to overstate effects. Every BCR is therefore shrunk toward break-even (BCR = 1) in log space, in proportion to its grade:

BCR̃={BCRkBCR>0k⋅BCRBCR≤0k=1−s(1−wg)\widetilde{BCR} = \begin{cases} BCR^{\,k} & BCR > 0 \\ k \cdot BCR & BCR \le 0 \end{cases} \qquad k = 1 - s(1 - w_g)

Here w_g is the grade weight, running from 1.00 for A+ down in steps of 0.05 to 0.60 for C−. The skepticism parameter s ∈ [0, 1] is set by the reader, with a default of 0.5.

Positive ratios shrink toward 1 in log space; zero or negative ratios shrink toward zero, that is, toward break-even and away from net harm. At s = 0 all numbers are taken at face value. At s = 1, a C− ratio keeps 60% of its magnitude in log terms, so a ratio of 100 becomes about 16, and a C− ratio of −1 becomes −0.6. The adjustment is a transparent heuristic in the spirit of Bayesian shrinkage toward a skeptical prior (Gelman et al., 2013). It is not a formal posterior.

Discounting. Published ratios are already discounted, mostly at 3–7%. To test other rates, benefits are assumed to arrive on average ten years after costs, and each ratio is multiplied by ((1 + 0.05)/(1 + r))^10, where r is the reader’s rate.

This is an approximation, because the underlying cash-flow profiles are not available for every study. For negative ratios the factor scales the net numerator, so it assumes that damages and benefits share the same timing. The rate range offered (0–10%) spans the 3% and 7% of OMB Circular A-4 (2003), which was reinstated in 2025 after the 2023 revision (2%) was rescinded (OMB, 2025), and the 3.5% of the UK Green Book (HM Treasury, 2022); see also Arrow et al. (2013).

Because the same factor multiplies every ratio, the discount rate does not reorder policies. It changes which policies clear the budget threshold in Section 3.11. A higher expected inflation rate implies a higher nominal discount rate.

3.8 Uncertainty analysis

Each published range is treated as the 90% interval of a lognormal distribution for the ratio. This is a standard choice for positive, right-skewed quantities (Morgan & Henrion, 1990). The log-mean is (ln L + ln H)/2, and the log-standard deviation is (ln H − ln L)/(2 × 1.645), with a floor of 0.10. Where a range crosses or touches zero, a normal distribution with the same 90% interval is used instead, with a floor of 0.05 on its standard deviation. Treating the spread of published estimates as a probability distribution converts disagreement between studies into sampling uncertainty; it is a pragmatic device, not a claim that the studies are random draws from one distribution.

The analysis draws N = 1,000 values per policy from the published range (random seed 42) and then applies the adjustments of Section 3.7 to each draw. For each draw, the full ranking is recomputed with the other criteria held fixed. This yields three outputs for each policy:

  1. the median adjusted BCR and its 5th–95th percentile interval;
  2. a 90% rank interval;
  3. the probability of ranking in the top 20.

With 1,000 draws, the Monte Carlo standard error of any reported probability is at most 1.6 percentage points (√(0.25/1000)).

Draws are independent across policies. Correlated uncertainty, for example between policies that share a mechanism or a source, is not modelled; this is a limitation.

3.9 Multi-criteria aggregation

All criteria are rescaled to [0, 1]:

  • Value: the signed log of the median adjusted BCR, sign(x) log10(1 + |x|), min-max rescaled.
  • Who benefits: 1 for mostly the poor, 0.5 for everyone, 0 for mostly higher incomes.
  • Feasibility: 1 for easy, 0.5 for moderate, 0 for hard.
  • Cost: 1 minus the rescaled log10(1 + annual cost).

Min-max rescaling makes the value criterion depend on the most extreme ratios in the set; adding or removing an extreme policy changes every policy’s scaled value, although not the order by value.

The score of policy i is:

Si=Vi+τ∑k∈{poor, feasibility, cost}tk(cik−0.5)S_i = V_i + \tau\sum_{k \in \{\text{poor, feasibility, cost}\}} t_k\,(c_{ik} - 0.5)

Here V_i is the value criterion, and t_k ∈ [−1, 1] is the reader’s tilt on criterion k, set by the sidebar dials with a default of 0. With τ = 0.3, one tilt can move a policy’s score by at most ±0.15 on the 0–1 value scale, so it can shift the gap between two policies by at most 0.3. With all three tilts at full strength the combined shift can reach 0.9, which is enough to reorder a large part of the ranking. Formally, the rule is a constrained weighted sum in which the weight on value is fixed at one.

This deliberately departs from the usual weighted-sum MCDA, in which the analyst or reader chooses weights for all criteria including value. In a pure weighted sum, the BCR could be outweighed entirely by subjective preferences. Here the published evidence always counts in full, and the tilts can reorder close calls but cannot overturn large differences in value.

An evidence-strength tilt is not offered, because evidence quality already enters through the skepticism adjustment (Section 3.7). The published ranking is the order of S_i at the default settings: s = 0.5, r = 5% and all tilts at 0. At these settings the tilt terms are zero, so the published ranking is simply the order of median adjusted BCRs. The multi-criteria layer is a tool for sensitivity analysis and for readers with different priorities, not a driver of the published result.

A full stochastic multicriteria acceptability analysis, which samples the weights as well (Lahdelma, Hokkanen & Salminen, 1998; Tervonen & Figueira, 2008), is left for future work.

3.10 Sensitivity analysis

Beyond the Monte Carlo analysis, the ranking was recomputed under nine alternative scenarios, following standard one-at-a-time and scenario practice (Saltelli et al., 2008):

  • the baseline;
  • no skepticism, and full skepticism;
  • discount rates of 2% and 7%;
  • full tilts toward the poor, toward easy policies, and toward cheap policies;
  • all three tilts together;
  • a source-dependence test that replaces the ranges of the two top-ranked trade policies with the most conservative estimates in the counter-evidence register: free trade 11 to 180 (Feyrer et al., 2023; Anderson, 2012) and agricultural subsidies 17 to 80 (the static estimates of Anderson & Winters, 2009).

Spearman’s rank correlation with the baseline is reported for each scenario, but it is a blunt measure: it can stay near one while the top of the ranking changes. The number of baseline top-ten policies that stay in the top ten, and the identity of the first-ranked policy, are therefore reported alongside it (Table 4). The best, median and worst scenario ranks of every policy are in the replication files.

3.11 Budget exercise

The headline budget is official development assistance from Development Assistance Committee donors: USD 174.3 billion in 2025 (OECD, 2026).

Best buys. Policies above a reader-chosen ratio threshold (default 1) are funded in descending order of median adjusted BCR. A policy is skipped if its cost no longer fits in the remaining budget, or if a higher-ranked member of its overlap group (Section 3.2) is already funded. This is a greedy solution to the budget-constrained selection (knapsack) problem, the usual heuristic in league-table allocation (Boardman et al., 2018). At the default threshold, all costed policies with a ratio above one fit within the budget, so the constraint does not bind and part of the budget is left unspent.

Counterfactual. The same amount that the best buys actually spend is split equally across the costed policies among the ten with the lowest ratios. These are mostly mandates proposed by national governments and international bodies. The equal split is a simple benchmark, not a forecast of how such policies would be funded; many of them are mandates whose costs fall on private parties rather than on aid budgets.

For both allocations, net value is spending × (BCR − 1). This is the present value of the benefits bought by one year’s spending, net of that spending. Reforms costed at zero add value without using the budget, so they are listed but not included in the dollar totals.

3.12 Software and reproducibility

All analysis was carried out in R 4.3.3 (R Core Team, 2024). The dashboard is built with shiny 1.14 and bslib 0.12 (Chang et al., 2024), and is compiled with shinylive 0.5 (Schloerke & Chang, 2024) to run in the reader’s web browser via webR, with no server. Figures use base R graphics.

The replication project (LH_CBA) contains:

  • the evidence file, with every range, grade, rating, source and piece of arithmetic;
  • the build scripts;
  • the analysis engine;
  • the sensitivity scripts;
  • the dashboard code.

Every result can be regenerated from these files with a fixed random seed; the session information is saved with the outputs.

Data and code availability. The evidence file, scripts, outputs and dashboard are provided in the replication package and online at https://www.tylerisyoung.com/cba-dashboard/. A permanent archive with a DOI will be deposited on publication.

Use of AI tools. AI research assistants were used to search for and summarise sources, draft source records and write code. Every numeric input and citation was checked against the source before use, and all analytic decisions are the author’s.

3.13 Limitations

  1. Heterogeneous sources. The ratios come from studies with different discount rates, horizons, price years, regions, standing and benefit concepts, and in some cases different definitions of costs. Some ratios divide permanent benefit flows by one-off adjustment costs, while others compare annual flows. Putting them on one scale is the purpose of the exercise, but it assumes they are comparable. Reporting net present values alongside ratios would help and is left for future work.
  2. Constructed and transferred ratios. Several ranges are constructed from published components or transferred from analogues rather than reported directly; the 9 policies graded C+ or below rest largely on such estimates. They are the most sensitive to the skepticism setting.
  3. Source selection. The search deliberately sought estimates of dynamic, long-run gains from market reforms, and sources from market-oriented institutes are more numerous in the register than sources from other perspectives. This is a real risk of bias. The counter-evidence register documents what was set aside and why, and the source-dependence test in Section 3.10 shows that the rank of the top trade policies depends on which trade estimates are used. Readers who weight the excluded studies more heavily can raise the skepticism setting or rebuild the ranges.
  4. Evidence grades. The rubric places published, quantified economic theory (B) above official government estimates (B−). This reflects the author’s judgement that official estimates are often static and politically constrained; other researchers may order these differently.
  5. Climate damages. Ratios for climate policies depend heavily on the social cost of carbon chosen by their sources, which ranges from about $30 to $190 per tonne. A scenario that harmonises the social cost of carbon across all climate policies is left for future work.
  6. Policy definitions. Policies are analysed as defined in their titles, some of which describe strong versions of a reform or a mandate. Milder versions may have very different ratios.
  7. Independence and overlap. Monte Carlo draws are independent across policies, although some policies share sources and should move together. Overlapping policies (Section 3.2) are not summed in the budget exercise.
  8. Zero-cost reforms. Repeals are costed at zero, following the transfer convention. Their private adjustment costs sit inside their ratios, and their benefits are not counted in the budget totals. The asymmetry with mandates is discussed in Section 3.6.
  9. Implementation. Feasibility ratings describe legal and institutional hurdles, not political probability. Ratios assume the policy is implemented as defined.

The Basel Committee (BCBS 2010) puts the annual probability of a banking crisis at ~4.5% and the median cumulative loss at 19% of GDP (no permanent effect) to 63% (all studies), so the expected annual crisis cost is 4.5% x 19% = 0.86% to 4.5% x 63% = 2.8% of GDP. (c) Benes & Kumhof (2012, IMF) model output gains from a 100%-reserve system 'approaching 10%'. COSTS: resource cost of commodity reserves, 0.5% of GDP (Meltzer 1983) to 0.249% of GDP (measured under the US classical gold standard, Watts & Snyder 2015). Low = (1.0% Lucas + 0.86% crisis, temporary losses) / 0.5% = 3.7. Central = (1.0% + 2.8%) / 0.249% = ~15. High = 10% (Benes & Kumhof) / 0.249% = 40; the Lagos-Wright + permanent-crisis-loss route gives (3% + 2.8%) / 0.249% = 23. 16,"Separation of State and Economics (constitutional amendment)","State/econ split","Governance & Tax",2,19,"No published BCR exists for a constitutional separation of state and economy, so the range uses the two peer-reviewed endogenous-growth estimates of what federal regulation has cost US output, set against the largest official estimate of the benefits regulation delivers.
